doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Rewriting Basie arrangements for a small group today
summary: He recently reduced fifteen Count Basie-band arrangements to three horns for a singer, finding errors in the scores.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. When we were corresponding through e-mail to set up this session you said, you wrote, “I’ve just finished a project and delivered the music on Sunday.” So my curiosity is how has delivering the project, the music, changed from the ‘60s until now for you?

Well when I said I delivered the music I worked on a record with the girl I work with. In fact tonight she’s doing a performance at Birdland. And she did this record with the Count Basie band and I had to modify the arrangements for three horns, because she couldn’t use the big band. So there were 15 arrangements that had to be re-written. So for small projects like that I would – it’s impossible to do the – it just becomes cost prohibitive if you get a copyist to do them so I sort of have a fee that I do them all myself
and I have the printed parts and she lives up the street. So I drove ten minutes up the street and dropped them off.
Did you have the Basie scores to work from or did you have to use your ear?

No I had the scores but there were a lot of mistakes in them and a lot of things that the musicians played that weren’t in the parts. And some of the arrangements – in fact it was difficult to try to work it out because a lot of the piano parts only had chords so if she went to perform where the piano wasn’t playing for four bars, there were rests. So I mean it’d have to be modified.
Yeah. I have a score or two that just crack me up because the arranger instead of writing “first alto” or whatever, they’d actually put the names down of the guys.
And I just – that’s history man, I love it.
Yeah well there were a couple of them that were written that way too.
